source_groups.label: Unequal astrological hours versus constant sixty-minute civil hours
claims: authorial_context
Ancients Winter and Summer equal hours
Lilly notes that some earlier authorities used equal 60-minute hours for day and night even in winter and summer.

method
Astrologians follow motion of Sun
He rejects constant-duration hours in favor of sunlight-dependent lengths.
The source requires solar times, not merely the weekday.
condition
Sun-rise to Sun-set twelve equal parts
The interval from sunrise to sunset is divided into exactly twelve equal daylight parts.
Equal within one day, usually unequal to civil hours.
condition
one half before Noon
Lilly describes six daylight planetary hours before noon.
His printed table separates first and second six hours.
condition
rest after Noon
Six remaining daylight planetary hours fall after noon.
Noon division assumes his table's solar convention.
condition
Sun-set until next Sun-rise twelve parts
The next night from sunset to sunrise is likewise divided into twelve equal nighttime parts.
Nighttime planetary hour length generally differs from daylight length.
source_qualification
more or less sixty minutes
Throughout most of the year a planetary hour can be longer or shorter than sixty minutes.
This is an arithmetic observation, not empirical astrology validation.
condition
Sun into Aries or Libra sixty minutes
Lilly says planetary-hour duration becomes exactly sixty minutes at solar ingress into Aries or Libra.
Equinox idealization; no modern local astronomical parity asserted.
